title: When did the Roman Empire fall?
hook: The school answer is 476. But half the empire kept going for almost another thousand years.
summary: In the West in 476, when Odoacer deposed the last emperor; in the East the empire lasted until 1453, and its people called themselves Romans.
cardText: It depends on which half. The Western Empire ended in 476. The Eastern one, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453, and its people called themselves Romans.

cardBlocks.text: In 476 the Germanic warrior Odoacer was proclaimed king by his troops in Italy and deposed Romulus Augustulus, a boy ruling in his father’s name. That date is usually taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire. But the eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, carried on without a break, with its laws, army and taxes.
That empire lasted almost another thousand years, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453. We call it Byzantine today, but its people didn’t use the name: they called themselves Romans.
Rome fell in the West in 476, but the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Romulus was the son of Orestes, a general who drove the emperor Julius Nepos out of Italy in 475 and put his son on the throne. His name, Augustus, became the diminutive Augustulus because he was still a child. The Eastern emperor never recognised him: to Constantinople he was a usurper.

Odoacer spared the boy because of his age, gave him a pension and sent him to live with relatives in Campania, in southern Italy. Nobody knows what became of him. Odoacer, for his part, recognised the authority of the Eastern emperor, Zeno, and changed little in how Italy was run. The fall was less a crash than a change of management.

In the sixth century the emperor Justinian gathered Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis and launched campaigns to win back Italy and North Africa, framed as reconquests of Roman land. Latin remained the official language of government until the seventh century, when Greek gradually took over.

In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople for 55 days before breaching its ancient walls. Even then its people called themselves Romans, and Ottoman sources called them Rum, a word that comes from “Roman”.
Where the name Byzantine came from

The name comes from Byzantium, the old Greek city that became Constantinople. It was popularised from the 16th century by Western European historians who wanted to keep the classical Rome they admired apart from a Greek-speaking Christian empire they distrusted. The term is usually credited to the German humanist Hieronymus Wolf, in 1557, but a recent study argues that “Byzantium” already appears in medieval sources, sometimes as a name for the empire itself.

claims.text: The name “Byzantine” comes from Byzantium, the old Greek name of Constantinople, and was popularised by early modern Western European historians.

support.excerpt: It derives from Byzantion, the ancient Greek name of Constantinople before it became the imperial capital. The label was popularized by early modern historians, particularly in Western Europe, who wished to separate the classical Roman past they admired from the Greek-speaking Christian empire they viewed with suspicion or disdain.
The latter term is derived from the name Byzantium, borne by a colony of ancient Greek foundation on the European side of the Bosporus

claims.text: The term is usually credited to Hieronymus Wolf in 1557, but a 2024 study argues that medieval sources already used “Byzantium”, sometimes for the empire.

support.excerpt: It is widely acknowledged that this designation, along with “Byzantine Empire”, was first introduced by the German historian and humanist Hieronymus Wolf in his “Corpus Historiae Byzantinae” in 1557.

However, the author of this study challenges this established view, contending that historical sources from both the Early and High Middle Ages, centuries prior to the Modern Age, contain references to “Byzantium”, sometimes even as name for the Eastern Roman Empire.
